meta.title: Proxmox Health Monitor — CPU, Memory, Storage, SMART, ZFS, Logs | ProxMenux
meta.description: Proactive Proxmox VE health monitoring: ten categories scanned every five minutes (CPU & temperature, memory & swap, storage, disks/SMART, network, VMs, services, logs, updates, security), four severity levels, per-category suppression durations, automatic cleanup of resolved errors, a permanent disk observation history and the path from a raw event to a Telegram, Discord, Gotify or email notification.

header.title: Health Monitor
header.description: The continuous self-check that scans ten categories of host state on a five-minute cycle, samples vital signs continuously between cycles, deduplicates findings into a structured event stream, and feeds the dashboard, the notification engine and the optional AI rewriter from one source of truth.

intro.title: One scanner, three consumers
intro.body: A background thread runs the full health cycle every 5 minutes, persists each finding into SQLite under a stable error_key, and lets (1) the dashboard render the current state, (2) the notification engine fan out new events to the configured channels, and (3) the optional AI assistant rewrite alerts in plain language. You configure the scanner once; everything downstream stays in sync.

howItWorks.heading: How it works
howItWorks.intro: The Health Monitor uses two parallel threads inside the Monitor process. A lightweight vital signs sampler fills CPU, memory and temperature history buffers. The full health cycle reads those buffers, evaluates sustained conditions and runs the other checks approximately every five minutes, then writes findings to SQLite for the dashboard and notification flow.
howItWorks.scannerCaption: The sampler fills history buffers between health cycles: CPU usage every 5 s, memory every 30 s and temperature every 15 s. It does not evaluate alerts itself. The full cycle evaluates those buffers and runs heavier checks (SMART, ZFS pool state, journal scanning and service health) before writing findings to SQLite.

categories.heading: The ten categories
categories.imageAlt: Health Monitor view showing the ten categories with their current statuses (CPU, Memory, Storage, Disks, Network, VMs, Services, Logs, Updates, Security)
categories.imageCaption: Health Monitor view — the ten categories with their current status. Categories on a healthy host all show OK; warnings and critical events appear inline with the rows that produced them.
categories.intro: Every cycle exercises ten independent checkers. Each produces one of four statuses (OK, INFO, WARNING, CRITICAL) plus a structured payload — device names, sample log lines, exact thresholds — that surface in the dashboard and travel through to the notification body.

rows.checks: CPU usage with hysteresis, sensor temperature
rows.events: Sustained high CPU usage; sensor-temperature warnings based on sampled readings.
Sustained memory pressure; OOM-killer activity; swap exhaustion.

Root or other monitored filesystems crossing configured space thresholds (85% warning / 95% critical by default); unavailable PVE storages; stale or unexpectedly read-only NFS/CIFS mounts; LVM-thin and other pool storages crossing the same thresholds.

rows.checks: SMART, dmesg I/O errors, ZFS pools, LVM, filesystem errors
rows.events: SMART health failed; reallocated / pending sectors; ATA I/O errors; ZFS pool DEGRADED / FAULTED; ext4 read-only remount.
Bridge or bond down; gateway unreachable; persistent latency spikes.

rows.checks: QMP communication, VM startup, container startup
rows.events: Failed VM boot; CT shutdown failure; QMP socket timeout; missing config / disk after a clone.
Service crashed; cluster quorum lost; pmxcfs stuck.

rows.checks: Persistent errors, error spikes, error cascades, critical kernel messages
rows.events: Repeated identical errors; sudden burst of warnings (cascade pattern); BUG: / OOPS: / oom-killer in dmesg.

rows.checks: Pending updates, security updates, kernel / PVE version, system age
rows.events: Pending security or running-kernel updates; a system not updated for a long time. The Updates category of the Health Status modal shows an Update Now button when updates are pending. It runs the full ProxMenux update flow inline; closing it refreshes health with ?refresh=1 so the badge reflects the new state without waiting for the next cycle.

rows.checks: Login attempts, certificates expiring, optional Fail2Ban jail status
rows.events: Repeated SSH / web auth failures; PVE certificate < 30 days from expiring; Fail2Ban active bans.

severity.heading: Severity model

rows.meaning: Healthy. No findings in this category.
Transient or already-resolved condition worth noting once. Also used for categories that have only dismissed items left.
rows.notification: Optional. Each event type can be opted in or out per channel.

rows.meaning: Attention is needed but the host is still functional. Cause is non-trivial — read the details.
rows.notification: Sent when the per-event toggle is on for the channel.

rows.meaning: Functionality broken or data loss possible. Action required.
rows.notification: Sent when the per-event toggle is on for the channel. CPU temperature CRITICAL is treated as a safety alert that re-fires even if previously dismissed.

severity.infoNote: A category that is OK but has dismissed events still inside their suppression window is rendered as INFO — to remind you that something is being silenced rather than that nothing was ever wrong.
severity.unknownTitle: UNKNOWN, when a check can't complete
severity.unknownBody: An unavailable check returns UNKNOWN; after three consecutive such cycles, a persistent finding is recorded. The dashboard shows an unavailable check in yellow. The overall view caps UNKNOWN at WARNING, so an unavailable check alone does not make the host CRITICAL.

dashboardView.heading: The dashboard view
dashboardView.intro: The Health Monitor lives inside the Overview tab. The header status pill (Healthy / Warning / Critical) opens a modal that splits findings into two lists:
items: Active — every category with an unresolved finding. Each row expands to show the individual checks that produced the status, the raw reason string, the device or VM ID involved, and (for categories that link to a tab) a click-through into Storage / Network / VMs / Logs / Hardware to investigate.

Dismissed — items previously acknowledged by the user that are still inside their suppression window. Each row shows how much of the suppression remains and the configured duration. When the window expires, the item disappears from this list; if the underlying condition is still present and the category supports re-firing, it re-appears in Active.
dashboardView.pillTitle: The pill mirrors the worst category
dashboardView.pillBody: The dashboard header colour is the highest severity across the ten categories: any CRITICAL → red, else any WARNING → yellow, else any INFO → blue, else green. The same logic drives the favicon dot and the PWA badge.
dashboardView.updateNowTitle: Update Now button in the Overview header
dashboardView.updateNowBody1: When the System Updates category reports one or more pending updates, the Overview header renders an Update Now button next to the health pill. The button opens a modal that runs the same host-side flow as ProxMenux → Settings post-install Proxmox → Proxmox System Update: repo hygiene, apt full-upgrade via the safe worker update-pve-safe.sh, automatic DKMS rebuild of ProxMenux-managed drivers when a new kernel lands, autoremove / autoclean and a reboot prompt if the kernel changed. Progress lines stream in the modal as the worker prints them.
dashboardView.updateNowBody2: When the run finishes, closing the modal calls GET /api/health/details?refresh=1, which invalidates the health-endpoint cache before serving. The pending-updates row and the pill severity are recomputed from the new package state on the spot, so the badge disappears without waiting for the next five-minute cycle. When the host is already up to date, the button is hidden — no visual noise on a healthy system.

dismiss.heading: Dismissing alerts and the Suppression Duration
dismiss.intro: Some events are noisy by nature — a System Updates: pending updates available stays true until you patch the host, and you don't want a notification every five minutes for a week. The Update Now button in the Updates category of the Health Status modal is the direct shortcut to resolve that specific case in place; for everything else, or when patching is deferred, the Health Monitor also offers two coupled silencing mechanisms:
dismiss.step1: Per-event Dismiss action in the modal. The Dismiss button opens a small dropdown with three options — 24 hours, 7 days or Permanently — letting you choose how long this specific alert stays silenced regardless of the category's default. Picking one calls POST /api/health/acknowledge with the error_key and the chosen suppression_hours (-1 for permanent). The event moves to the Dismissed list with a timestamped acknowledged_at.
dismiss.dropdownImageAlt: Dismiss dropdown on a Health Monitor alert — 24 hours, 7 days or Permanently
dismiss.dropdownImageCaption: Per-event Dismiss dropdown. The chosen window applies to this single alert; without a per-event choice the category default is used. Permanent dismissals have an amber Permanent badge and normally do not re-fire. The critical CPU-temperature override described below is an exception.
dismiss.step2: Per-category Suppression Duration setting. From the Settings → Health Monitor card (or POST /api/health/settings), each of the ten categories has its own default window applied when a Dismiss is fired without a per-event choice:
dismiss.imageAlt: Per-category Suppression Duration settings card in Settings → Health Monitor
dismiss.imageCaption: Suppression Duration card — one dropdown per category. Pick a longer window for noisy events (e.g. pending updates) and shorter for ones you want to re-evaluate quickly. Active Suppressions are listed underneath (see below).
dismiss.outro: While an event is suppressed, the scanner still runs and updates the row's last_seen timestamp, but no new notification is dispatched and the dashboard stays calm. When the window expires, the next cycle re-evaluates the condition and either re-fires fresh or, if the condition has cleared on its own, drops the row from the lists.
dismiss.activeSuppressionsTitle: Reviewing and reverting dismisses — the Active Suppressions panel
dismiss.activeSuppressionsBody: Every currently-silenced alert (time-limited and permanent) is listed under Settings → Health Monitor → Active Suppressions. Each row shows the alert identifier, category, severity, when it was dismissed and how much time is left, plus a Re-enable button that clears the acknowledgment so the alert can fire again on the next scan. Permanent dismisses can only be reverted from here; time-limited ones can also be force-revived without waiting for the countdown. The Re-enable action is gated by the Health Monitor Edit mode at the top of that card — toggle Edit, click Re-enable on each row you want to revive (queued rows show a green border and a strike-through), then click Save to commit. Cancel discards the queue.
dismiss.autoTitle: Auto-suppression when you change the Duration
dismiss.autoBody: Setting a category's Suppression Duration to anything other than the default 24 h has a second effect beyond user-initiated dismissals: future findings in that category enter the table already acknowledged with that duration. This is by design — if you've told the Monitor that you want disk-related events silenced for a week, brand-new disk findings honour that intent without you having to dismiss each one by hand. They appear directly in the Dismissed list with the configured remaining time. Categories left at 24 h are unaffected and behave the classic way (new findings land in Active until you act).
dismiss.tempTitle: CPU temperature CRITICAL is the safety override
dismiss.tempBody: The persistence layer has a special guard for a record marked CPU temperature CRITICAL: if such a record is received, it bypasses prior acknowledgment and auto-suppression. This guard does not mean that every temperature checker emits a critical record whenever a configured critical threshold is crossed.
dismiss.nonDismissableBody: The modal shows Dismiss only when an individual check explicitly returns dismissable = true. A false or missing flag hides that button. Severity alone does not determine this permission: several critical checks allow acknowledgment. The examples below describe the current payloads; silencing an alert does not repair its cause.

rows.why: The sampled sensor-temperature warning explicitly allows dismissal. A separate persistence guard bypasses acknowledgment if a CPU-temperature record arrives with CRITICAL severity.
Filesystem-space checks explicitly allow dismissal, including critical usage. Acknowledging the alert does not free space or remove the risk of failed writes.
ZFS pool-state findings (DEGRADED, FAULTED, UNAVAIL) explicitly allow dismissal, as do pool-capacity checks. Acknowledgment does not repair a degraded or faulted pool.

rows.finding: Disk I/O errors with SMART FAILED
rows.why: Persisted journal-derived disk findings can allow dismissal. SMART FAILED still needs investigation; whether the button appears depends on the individual check flag, not on the alert text alone.
Persisted interface-DOWN checks explicitly allow dismissal. This does not restore a bridge, bond or physical link, or recover remote access.
Transient ATA or dmesg events with healthy SMART can be informational and self-clearing. Informational rows need not expose a Dismiss button; the checker determines when the condition is resolved.

dismiss.principle: Use the button shown for the actual finding, rather than inferring availability from its category or severity. Acknowledgment controls alert presentation and notifications; recovery checks and disk history remain separate.

autoresolve.heading: Auto-resolution and cleanup
autoresolve.intro: Many alerts should clear themselves when the condition goes away — a VM that was failing to start and is now running, a disk that's no longer in the system, a temperature that dropped back to normal. A cleanup routine runs at the end of each five-minute cycle and applies these rules:

rows.trigger: CPU usage back to normal range after a CPU-related warning.
rows.action: Marked resolved. Drops out of the Active list.

rows.trigger: Memory pressure back below the warning threshold after an OOM / memory warning.
VM / CT referenced by the error no longer exists (qm status / pct status non-zero).
Disk referenced by the error no longer present in /dev/.
rows.action: Marked resolved as device removed. The permanent observation history is preserved (see next section).

rows.trigger: Findings sourced from the journal (logs category, SMART entries, ATA / I/O errors) when their suppression window expires.
rows.action: Removed cleanly. Each scan inspects fresh journal entries from that point forward; the same historic line in the journal is not re-emitted.

rows.trigger: Resolved errors older than seven days.
rows.action: Deleted from the database to keep the table small. Notification history is independent and kept longer.

autoresolve.permanentTitle: Permanent suppression is not the same as resolved
autoresolve.permanentBody: Setting a category's Suppression Duration to -1 (permanent) silences future alerts for items you dismiss in that category — but it does not skip the auto-resolve check above. If the underlying condition disappears (resource deleted, threshold no longer breached), the item is still cleaned up automatically.

observations.heading: Disk observations — the permanent history
observations.intro: Disk events are special. A SMART warning on /dev/sdh at 02:14 AM is something you want to remember even after the I/O storm subsided and the error auto-resolved — the disk has a track record now. For that purpose, the Health Monitor keeps a separate permanent table: disk_observations.

rows.errors: Drives the current health view + notification dispatch.
Yes — rows are cleared when the condition disappears.
rows.obs: No — entries persist forever unless the user explicitly dismisses them.
(disk_registry_id, error_type, error_signature) with stable signatures stripped of volatile data.
Disk detail card in the Storage tab, with an "X obs." badge per disk.
SMART warnings (sector issues / temperature / CRC / failed self-tests), I/O errors (ATA / NVMe / dm), filesystem errors, ZFS pool events.

observations.outro: Practical consequence: an alert can clear from the dashboard while the same incident is still recorded in the disk's history. When you click into a disk under Storage, the card shows the count of outstanding observations and a list with timestamps, severity and the original raw message — useful when you're deciding whether a drive needs replacement.
observations.renameBody: Disks sometimes appear under transient names (ata8, nvme0n1p3) before getting a stable block-device name. The observation layer consolidates entries by serial number when known: if an event was first recorded as ata8 and the same disk is later identified as sdh, the historic observations are reattached to sdh on the next cycle so the history isn't fragmented.

notification.heading: From a finding to a notification
notification.intro: Every active error is also a candidate for the notification engine. The flow:
items: The scanner records the finding with category + severity + structured details.
If the event type is enabled in the global notification settings, and the channel hasn't silenced this category, an event is queued.
The template engine renders a (title, body) pair from the structured details. If the AI rewriter is enabled, the same pair is also passed through the configured provider for a plain-language version.
The channel implementation ships it: Telegram message, Discord embed, Gotify push or email. The dispatch outcome is stored in notification_history.

Dismissing an alert starts its suppression window. Further detections of the same error_key normally produce no new notification during that window; they are not automatically queued for delivery when it ends. The critical CPU-temperature override remains an exception.
notification.outro: Channel configuration (Telegram bot token, webhook URLs, AI provider keys, per-event toggles, channel overrides) is documented in <notifLink>Notifications</notifLink> and <aiLink>AI Assistant</aiLink>.

rest.heading: REST endpoints
rest.intro: The modal actions are also available through the API for scripts, custom dashboards or chatbots. Calls need a valid bearer token, either from login or the API-token screen. Changes such as acknowledging alerts, saving suppression settings or cleaning orphan errors require full_admin scope; read_only receives 403.

rows.use: Lightweight health probe returning JSON with status, timestamp and version. Suitable for Uptime Kuma keyword checks; the client must send a bearer header.
Overall health verdict — single severity + summary string. Authenticated.
All ten categories with their per-category statuses and the structured payload that produced each one.
Full snapshot — categories + active errors + dismissed list + custom suppression settings. Backs the modal in one round-trip and uses a 6-min background cache for instant response.
Just the Active list. Filterable by ?category=<name>.
Just the Dismissed list, with remaining suppression hours.
Body: '{'"error_key":"smart_sdh"'}'. Dismiss an alert with the category's configured window.
Read or write the per-category Suppression Duration values.
Manual cleanup of errors whose underlying device / VM is gone. Idempotent.
